finding.claim: reset_password_loose compares the stored reset token with the loose `==` operator. PHP type juggling lets an attacker match a token without knowing it. If the stored token is a numeric-looking string such as '0e12345', any other '0e...' string compares equal. If the caller passes a JSON-decoded value, `true` equals any non-empty string. Either way the attacker resets the password of any account by email. The function is a loose twin of the safe reset_password, and nothing shows it is unused.
finding.source: Attacker-controlled $email and $token arguments, presumably from a password-reset HTTP request. $token may be a JSON bool or int if the caller decodes JSON, or a '0e...' string.
finding.sink: UPDATE users SET pw = ... WHERE email = ... at reset.php:5, which overwrites the victim's password hash.

trace.note: The stored token is fetched by the attacker-supplied email.
`$row['token'] == $token` uses loose comparison, so type juggling and magic-hash collisions pass the check.
The password hash is overwritten for the target email.

finding.guards_checked: Checked for strict comparison, hash_equals, a (string) cast, token expiry, rate limiting and a caller-side type check. None exist on this path. The SQL values are escaped with $db->quote, so there is no SQL injection. The caller is not in the repo, so exploitability depends on how $token is typed and what format stored tokens have.

verdict.guard_found: none in reset.php; no strict comparison, cast, expiry or rate limit, and the SQL is quoted with $db->quote (reset.php:3, 5-6). The safe twin at reset.php:14 uses hash_equals with a (string) cast, but nothing in the repo calls either function.
verdict.reason: The loose `==` at reset.php:4 is real and the trace is accurate, but no caller exists in the repo (grep finds only the two definitions at reset.php:2 and :12). Exploitability depends on whether $token can arrive as a JSON bool or int, or whether stored tokens look like '0e...'. Neither can be determined from the code available.

finding.claim: Neither reset function expires or consumes the token. A successful reset leaves the row in `resets`, so the same token works again until something else deletes it. The code also stores no creation time, so tokens never expire, and it has no attempt limiting, so tokens can be brute-forced. A leaked or intercepted token gives permanent account takeover.
finding.source: Attacker who obtains or guesses a reset token for a victim's email. Leak routes include logs, referrer headers, email compromise and old emails.
finding.sink: UPDATE users SET pw = ... at reset.php:15. The same token works on every later call.

trace.note: The token is looked up by email only. There is no expiry or used-flag filter.
The token is verified in constant time, but nothing limits the number of attempts.
The password is updated. No DELETE or invalidation of the resets row follows.

finding.guards_checked: Checked for token deletion after use, an expiry timestamp column, attempt throttling and a lockout. None are present in this file. The code that issues tokens and the caller are not in the repo, so a cleanup job or other control could exist elsewhere.

verdict.guard_found: none in this file: hash_equals at reset.php:14 only does constant-time comparison; no DELETE/used flag, no expiry column, no attempt limiting. Token issuance and callers are not in the repo.
verdict.reason: reset.php:13 selects the token by email only, reset.php:14 compares it with hash_equals and nothing limits attempts, and reset.php:15 updates the password with no deletion or invalidation of the resets row, so a token can be reused indefinitely (the claim that tokens can be brute-forced rests on the unseen issuance code's token entropy, and a cleanup job elsewhere is possible but not visible).
